Before you follow steps in this page to deploy, manage, back up or restore etcd,
you need to understand the typical expectations for operating an etcd cluster.
candidates.title: configure-upgrade-etcd

candidates.text:
Ensure that the leader
  periodically send heartbeats on time to all followers to keep the cluster
  stable.
candidates.title: configure-upgrade-etcd

candidates.text:
Performance and stability of the cluster is sensitive to network and disk
  I/O.
candidates.title: configure-upgrade-etcd

candidates.text:
Any resource starvation can lead to heartbeat timeout, causing instability
  of the cluster.
candidates.title: configure-upgrade-etcd

candidates.text: An unstable etcd indicates that no leader is elected.
candidates.title: configure-upgrade-etcd

candidates.text:
Under
  such circumstances, a cluster cannot make any changes to its current state,
  which implies no new pods can be scheduled.
candidates.title: configure-upgrade-etcd

candidates.text:
For Kubernetes, the _Metrics API_ offers a basic set of metrics to support automatic scaling and
similar use cases.
candidates.title: resource-metrics-pipeline

candidates.text:
This API makes information available about resource usage for node and pod,
including metrics for CPU and memory.
candidates.title: resource-metrics-pipeline

candidates.text:
If you deploy the Metrics API into your cluster, clients of
the Kubernetes API can then query for this information, and you can use Kubernetes' access control
mechanisms to manage permissions to do so.
candidates.title: resource-metrics-pipeline

candidates.text:
You can also view the resource metrics using the
[`kubectl top`](/docs/reference/generated/kubectl/kubectl-commands#top)
command.
candidates.title: resource-metrics-pipeline

candidates.text:
The Metrics API, and the metrics pipeline that it enables, only offers the minimum
CPU and memory metrics to enable automatic scaling using HPA and / or VPA.
candidates.title: resource-metrics-pipeline

candidates.text: Figure 1 illustrates the architecture of the resource metrics pipeline.
candidates.title: resource-metrics-pipeline

candidates.text:
Resource metrics are accessible using the `/metrics/resource` and `/stats` kubelet
  API endpoints.
candidates.title: resource-metrics-pipeline

candidates.text:
The API server serves Metrics API for use by HPA, VPA, and by
  the `kubectl top` command.
candidates.title: resource-metrics-pipeline

candidates.text: Metrics Server is a reference implementation of the Metrics API.
candidates.title: resource-metrics-pipeline

candidates.text:
To make this work in your cluster, you need an API extension server that
  provides the Metrics API.
candidates.title: resource-metrics-pipeline

candidates.text:
By default, the `hosts` file only includes IPv4 and IPv6 boilerplates like
`localhost` and its own hostname.
candidates.title: customize-hosts-file-for-pods

candidates.text: Adding entries to a Pod's `/etc/hosts` file provides Pod-level override of hostname resolution when DNS and other options are not applicable.
candidates.title: customize-hosts-file-for-pods

candidates.text: You can add these custom entries with the HostAliases field in PodSpec.
candidates.title: customize-hosts-file-for-pods

candidates.text:
The Kubernetes project recommends modifying DNS configuration using the `hostAliases` field
(part of the `.spec` for a Pod), and not by using an init container or other means to edit `/etc/hosts`
directly.
candidates.title: customize-hosts-file-for-pods

candidates.text: Change made in other ways may be overwritten by the kubelet during Pod creation or restart.
candidates.title: customize-hosts-file-for-pods
